items.title: [ArchDaily] The Kitchen Edge: Service, Storage, and Domestic Boundaries in Compact Interiors
items.content_html: In compact homes, the kitchen is rarely only a room for cooking. It often operates as an edge: a service wall or a boundary between domestic work and social life. Its importance lies not only in food preparation, but in how it organizes the rest of the home, particularly due to limitations of plumbing and ventilation requirements. Before a living room can feel open, the kitchen often has to absorb the practical intensity of daily life: water, heat, smell, appliances, groceries, and storage.

items.title: [ArchDaily] From Residual Land to Civic Places: 6 Mexican Public Parks
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Mexico's rapid urban growth over recent decades has left many cities struggling with fragmented neighborhoods, high crime rates, and severe shortages of quality public spaces. In many low-income urban areas, informal development occurred alongside raw infrastructure like drainage canals, rail lines, and steep ravines, dividing communities and creating hazardous vacant zones. To address this spatial segregation and lack of civic amenities, public agencies and architects across Mexico are intervening in these abandoned buffer zones to construct public parks. By converting former physical barriers into accessible pedestrian corridors, these projects rejoin separated neighborhoods, re-establish safe visual sight lines, and provide spaces for community gathering and daily recreation.

items.title: [ArchDaily] The Makers Barn Residence / HUTCH design
items.content_html: Once an abandoned piggery, now a fine example of elemental architecture, The Makers Barn goes to great lengths to honour its agricultural origins. Borrowing its robust pitched roof from the nearby Tudor cottages—and clad with vertical larch planks—the barn cuts a utilitarian silhouette against a meadow of tall grasses and wildflowers on London's rural fringe. Built for play and purpose, it's the kind of environ that causes its inhabitants to feel well.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Building the India of the Imagination: Cinema and the Making of Place
items.content_html: Some of India's most convincing architectural worlds have never existed outside a film set. Courtyards, palaces, streets and even entire neighbourhoods have been constructed, lit and framed for the camera, then dismantled when filming ends. Their images remain. For millions of viewers, these spaces become references for how cities look, how wealth is displayed and how particular neighbourhoods or versions of India are remembered. Cinema constructs spatial worlds, compressing complex histories into images that audiences can recognise almost instantly. Those images can later shape how physical places are understood.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Chengdu Haiyang Road Middle School / Changwu Architects
items.content_html: When most urban campuses are compressed into efficiency-first functional containers, Chengdu Haiyang Road Middle School seeks to cultivate the relaxed, leisurely atmosphere of Chengdu's iconic "Wide and Narrow Alleys," reclaiming a sense of freedom for bodies otherwise disciplined by efficiency. There are no rigid corridors here, only staggered streets and alleys, light and shadow that are relevant to the body, a second-floor platform where you can chase the sunset, and the insistence that "every courtyard has a tree". As Louis Kahn famously said, education begins with a conversation under a tree. On this campus, gently dappled with shifting shadows, learning no longer happens only in classrooms, but also in every aimless wandering and discovery.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Luke Mitchell on Design Process
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

🔧 ✏️

Tell us a little bit about yourself

I have been a designer of one sort or another since 2011. I started out as a Graphic Designer who also built websites, but as I got more and more interested in web apps and websites I started moving towards digital design then product design.

I am currently Lead Product Designer at Definely. I am happy working on design at any step of the process, whether that be strategy, research, prototyping, testing, design systems, and everything in between.

I also love to code when I get the chance, I am a big fan of HTML and CSS, but I will give most languages a try.

What are the first questions you ask at the beginning of every project?

  • What research do we already have?
  • Has any design work already been done?
  • What resources do we have to share?
  • Where did this idea come from? (support ticket, stakeholders etc.)
  • How urgent is it? (should I drop other things I’m working on to start on this?)
  • Who is the team that will be working on it?

How do you approach pricing with clients? How did you arrive at this?

I’ve never been freelance or been directly involved in too many pricing conversations, but I often need to estimate how long things will take. I usually start with a broad estimate followed by frequent updates, I like to over estimate and then take anything ahead of schedule as a win.

What are the first things you do when you start a new project?

I don’t usually do anything concrete, and it depends on the project. But I will usually start by ask a bunch of questions, and then outline the next steps I will take. I will try and learn as much as I can about the problem, from there I see where the wind takes me and go from there.

What does your moodboarding process look like? Where do you source inspiration?

I don’t moodboard as often I as used to, but when I do my sources vary. I tend to avoid just moodboarding bits of UI/UX, as that has too much of a bias for solutions. Instead I try to find an eclectic mix of sources, my favourites include architecture, interior design, photography, typography, and physical product design.

I read a lot articles from blogs and sites I like via RSS, and I save visuals I find inspiring on Savee.

What’s your favourite part of the design process? Why?

Prototyping. It’s great to move fast and get something out of your head, then test it with people quickly. I would love to have a number on the amount of hours I’ve saved on circular discussions about features by just building a little thing and showing it to people, it clarifies and validates faster than any amount of meetings could.

Are there any parts of your process that go against received wisdom? Or common steps that you skip? Why?

There have been times where I followed the ‘double diamond’ process religiously, but more often than not I tend to let the process reveal itself as move along. It really depends on the feature or product, but I find you can often skip a super in-depth discovery process for something far less formal and time consuming.

Similarly I often find that having a long iterative process of design drafts doesn’t really lead anywhere productive, sometimes shifting focus too much into detail too early in a project. I prefer to research to confirm assumptions, and then iterate on a shipped feature instead of iterating before launching anything at all.

Less double diamond and more squiggly line.

Is there anything else you suspect is unique or unusual about your practice?

I create lots of diagrams, which I don’t see very often from designers, I see it more from engineers and developers: Information architecture, user flows, workflows, swimlanes, all sorts. I think that it helps to get information structured and out of my head without a UI early. It really helps to focus on all those little words and connections, when you aren’t biased by colours, layout typography etc.

If you collaborate with others (copywriters, illustrators, developers, etc): when do you bring them in? How do you handle project management?

Early and often, if they’re curious to get involved. It can be very helpful to have a small team involved throughout the whole process. There have been plenty of times where a developer has asked a key question during a research interview, or a product manager has noticed an early inefficiency in my thinking, that would not have been caught until we were much further along otherwise.

What’s been the most impactful change you’ve made to your process? Where did you hear about it?

Asking “stupid” questions. I have learnt so much by asking questions that should have an obvious answer, and avoided massive assumptions early on. For example say somebody I’ve never worked with before mentions a “customer”, I will ask “What does ‘customer’ mean?”. The answer is often far more nuanced and unexpected than you might think.

Unfortunately I can’t remember where or when I first started doing this.

What parts of the process are non-negotiables for you?

Honestly, I’m happy to skip any part if there is a good reason to do so. I often have strong opinions on validating assumptions, and prototyping, but even those can be ditched in some projects.

How do you organise design files?

I’m not very good at this. I will occasionally have a blitz and a tidy up when things get overwhelming inside Figma. But if I’m handing anything over I’ll usually create a page with the name of a Linear ticket, and send links to that out.

What does design hand-off look like for you?

It depends on what I’m designing, if it’s a little change all that needed is a quick comment or Slack message. But as things get more complex I will document more heavily and write specs as needed, I’m not a pixel-perfect kind of guy.

I will also have short calls with the team and present the design and answer questions as they come up, and then document that instead if the feature is particularly big. I will often get involved directly with front-end code also if it saves a developer putting up with me listing 50 ‘snags’ that I’d like fixed.

Looking back over the last 12 months, how do people find out about you?

I’m not much of a self-promoter, I get a fair bit of traffic to my website, especially the bookmarks page, but it’s not something I actively push or post about anywhere else. I’m lucky to only have had to look for work once or twice in the last 10 years, both times I applied for those jobs. If I were ever to go freelance I would have to be much more proactive.

What elements of the process create speed bumps or challenges? How do you get out of these ruts?

I find projects often get stuck in a discussion loop, or lose momentum when the task seems a bit too big. I try to break that loop by doing or building something demonstrable that everyone can see, critique, and plan against. It’s easier to say if something works or doesn’t, or if it’s too ambitious, if you can see and use it.

How do you make decisions?

There are lots of factors to take into account for decision-making: time, urgency, impact etc. If it’s a short-term, low-impact, urgent decision I usually use experience and intuition to get those out of the way quickly. I know that the decision I make there is probably reversible and I can iterate on it later.

The trickier ones are the decisions where I care much more about the outcome, usually because it has long-term impact that would be hard to reverse quickly. In those cases I have to make sure I am prepared to answer any questions that might counter my opinion, I also like to be prepared with resources to back my decision up. If I can’t justify my decision with anything more than “because I think it’s right”, then I haven’t done my job.

That being said I am surrounded by smart people who I listen to when making decisions, and while I will push back I will concede or compromise when others have similarly well prepared arguments to mine.

Favourite tool, resource or course?

Physical: A nice pen and a nice notebook.

Digital: Things by Cultured Code.

Where can people find out more about you, keep up to date, or work with you?

Checkout my website, there are some other links on there: interroban.gg

items.title: Escapism in Architecture: ArchDaily's September Editorial Focus
items.content_html: At a moment when architects across the globe are revisiting earthen construction, reassessing vernacular technologies, and forging visceral connections between communities and the land beneath their feet, others are sketching habitats for the Moon and designing the built environments of a Martian colony. Architecture firms, engineers, and space agencies are investing serious intellectual effort into structures that would need to be raised from scratch on another world. Two impulses, one returning to the soil, the other reaching for the stars, are unfolding simultaneously within the same discipline. And the tension between them raises an uncomfortable question: what, exactly, are we trying to escape?

items.title: [ArchDaily] Climate Infrastructure at Human Scale: From Water Management to Urban Cooling
items.content_html: Water management, air quality, and heat mitigation are usually planned through systems much larger than the spaces where people actually experience them. Drainage networks sit below the street. Air pollution is measured across entire cities. Yet these conditions are felt much closer to the body: while waiting for a bus in the sun, walking through a flooded street, crossing an exposed plaza, or looking for somewhere to sit when the air itself feels difficult to breathe.

items.title: [ArchDaily] The Yakisugi Cabin / Alki Architecture + Design Studio
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Yakisugi Cabin explores architecture shaped by what is already available — where material constraint becomes a generative design tool rather than a limitation. Conceived as a compact, relocatable dwelling, the project brings together reclaimed materials, traditional craft and contemporary high-performance construction to test how lightly a building can occupy both its site and its wider material landscape.

items.title: [ArchDaily] The Balearic Social Housing Model Receives the 2026 OBEL Award
items.content_html: Amid growing economic, political, and climatic instability, the 2026 OBEL Award highlights the need for architectural approaches that rethink both existing and emerging infrastructures. The title for this edition is "Systems' Hack," where "systems" are understood as interrelated mechanisms governed by shared rules and "hacking" is framed as a strategic intervention that seeks to alter how these mechanisms operate. Within this framework, the OBEL Foundation has announced the Balearic Social Housing Model as the winner of this year's award, while also announcing a new cycle in 2027 under the same topic. The Balearic Social Housing Model is recognized for "transforming the role of social housing administration in the Balearic Islands between 2019 and 2023," proposing new approaches in response to an acute housing shortage and a critically limited public rental housing stock in Spain.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Rouxinol House / Sergio Sampaio Archi + Tectônica
items.content_html:
Concept
The 2,000-square-meter site of Rouxinol House, located in the Paraíba Valley in São Paulo, presented significant challenges in defining the architectural design. While it offered magnificent views of the Jaguari River reservoir, the design also had to address a 50-meter slope and the presence of over 300 surveyed trees. Minimizing environmental impact was non-negotiable—a combination of factors that determined the design decisions from the initial concept to the specification of materials.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Akina House / Di Frenna Arquitectos
items.content_html: Casa Akina announces itself without fully revealing its form. Its presence is restrained, almost silent. Before showing its true shape, it lets the light filter through, allows the vegetation to peek out, and hints at the central void that organizes it. From the very first encounter, the architecture proposes a deliberate pace of living, where the journey matters as much as the destination and time becomes perceptible.

items.title: [ArchDaily] The City as a System of Health: Breaking Feedback Loops in Planning
items.content_html: The spatial consequences of urban form are revealed when health outcomes are mapped over neighborhoods. Neighborhoods that support walking, daily errands, social interaction, and access to essential services create opportunities to incorporate physical activity into routine tasks. Places that are organized around long distances and automobile travel suppress this opportunity. Physical activity and the motivation to incorporate it into daily life are shaped by the distance to a grocery store, the safety of a pedestrian crossing, the frequency of public transportation, the width of a sidewalk, and the quantity of services within walking distance.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Weekend Villa / R+R Architects
items.content_html: Set against the tranquil outskirts of Ahmedabad, the Weekend Villa is envisioned as a contemporary weekend retreat that blurs the boundaries between resort living and residential comfort. Conceived as an immersive sanctuary, the villa draws deeply from Balinese tropical architecture while remaining rooted in a distinctly modern Indian context. The result is a home that celebrates leisure, craftsmanship, and an evocative material palette through a carefully choreographed spatial experience.

items.title: [ArchDaily] M+ Hong Kong Exhibition Traces Herzog & de Meuron's Design Process Across China
items.content_html: An exhibition tracing the vision behind Herzog & de Meuron's ten selected projects in China will open on September 12, 2026, at the M+ Museum in Hong Kong. The exhibition marks the museum's fifth anniversary; since opening, M+ has built its collection around visual art, design and architecture, moving image, and Hong Kong visual culture from the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. The museum building, designed by Herzog & de Meuron between 2012 and 2021, is located in the city's West Kowloon Cultural District (WestK), a cultural hub spanning forty hectares alongside Victoria Harbour. "Herzog & de Meuron: In Focus" is curated by Ikko Yokoyama and Iris Ng and reviews projects dating from 2002 to 2021, including Tai Kwun in Hong Kong (2006–2018) and the National Stadium in Beijing (2002–2008).

items.title: [ArchDaily] House in Hino / Shigeo Takizawa Architects
items.content_html: This house for a couple and their child stands in a quiet residential neighborhood developed on the Tama Hills during the 1960s. Formed by cutting into a north-facing slope, the surrounding landscape is marked by retaining walls and boundary fences—traces of the long struggle to create level ground for habitation. Benefiting from generous plots compared with those in central Tokyo and a building coverage ratio of 40%, the neighboring houses share a common disposition: large south-facing gardens and aligned facades.

Our goal was to create a place for the local community with inspiring architecture and environmental awareness - energy-efficient, based on renewable resources, using low-emission, natural materials, and blending into the surrounding nature and local context.
